paragraphs: Even if I conceded everything I have been arguing against, the friends of despotism would be no better off. Subduing a multitude is always very different from governing a society. Say that one man enslaves scattered individuals one after another, however many there are: I still see only a master and his slaves. I do not see a people and its ruler. What I see is what may be called an aggregation, not an association; there is as yet neither public good nor body politic. That man may have enslaved half the world, but he is still a single individual, and his interest, apart from everyone else’s, is still purely private. When he dies, his empire remains scattered and without unity, the way an oak collapses into a pile of ashes once fire has burned through it.

Grotius says that a people can give itself to a king. By that reasoning, a people is already a people before it gives itself away. The giving is itself a civil act, and it presupposes public deliberation. So before we examine how a people gives itself to a king, we should examine how it became a people in the first place. That earlier act must come first, and it is the true foundation of society.

Indeed, if there were no earlier convention, where would the minority’s obligation to accept the majority’s choice come from, unless the election were unanimous? What right have a hundred men who want a master to vote on behalf of ten who do not? The rule of majority voting is itself established by convention, and it presupposes unanimity on at least one occasion.
